entities.summary:
Matteo Rosso Orsini (died September 12, 1305) was a formidable Roman aristocrat, cardinal of the Catholic Church, and a pivotal political and diplomatic figure during the late 13th and early 14th centuries. A scion of the powerful Orsini family, his career epitomized the intertwined nature of Roman noble power, papal authority, and international diplomacy in Medieval Italy. His elevation to Cardinal Deacon of Santa Maria in Portico in 1262 by Pope Urban IV, despite his later close relationship with his uncle Pope Nicholas III, underscores his early prominence, securing his family's continued influence over the Holy See during a period of intense political maneuvering between Guelph and Ghibelline factions.

Throughout his long tenure as a cardinal, Orsini was deeply involved in the complex political landscape of the Papal States and beyond. He participated in at least nine papal conclaves, including the contentious election of 1268–1271, which ultimately led to the election of Pope Gregory X, and the pivotal 1294 conclave that saw the abdication of Pope Celestine V and the election of Pope Boniface VIII. Orsini served as Rector of the Marches of Ancona and Romagna, directly governing significant papal territories and asserting papal authority against local potentates and imperial claims. His diplomatic missions extended to France and England, where he mediated disputes and represented papal interests, showcasing his broad political acumen and influence across Europe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Matteo Rosso Orsini's long cardinalate and political acumen secured his powerful Orsini family's influence within the Roman Curia for decades, directly shaping numerous papal elections and the administration of the Papal States during a tumultuous era. His actions facilitated the rise and fall of several popes and maintained a consistent noble presence at the highest levels of the Church.
